raw_prompt: I want to publish an e-book on amazon. I have a file story.txt and ten pictures (picture1, picture2, picture3, etc..) what would a python script need in order to convert my files into a kindle format?
prompt_sent: I want to publish an e-book on amazon. I have a file story.txt and ten pictures (picture1, picture2, picture3, etc..) what would a python script need in order to convert my files into a kindle format?
response_text:
For Amazon KDP today, I would have the Python script generate a clean **EPUB**, then validate it with **Kindle Previewer**. Amazon accepts EPUB files that meet its Kindle Publishing Guidelines, and Kindle Create/Kindle Previewer can produce or preview Kindle-ready output. Amazon’s own KDP docs also say KPF is preferred when using Kindle Create, but Python scripts usually create EPUB because KPF is Amazon’s tool-generated publishing package, not a normal open format you hand-author directly. Sources: [KDP supported eBook formats](https://kdp.amazon.com/en_US/help/topic/G200634390), [KDP manuscript formatting guide](https://kdp.amazon.com/en_US/help/topic/G200645680), [Kindle Create guide](https://kdp.amazon.com/en_US/help/topic/GUGQ4WDZ92F733GC), [Kindle Previewer user guide](https://kindlepreviewer3.s3.amazonaws.com/UserGuide320_EN.pdf). **Recommended Workflow** Your script should produce: ```text story.txt + picture1.jpg ... picture10.jpg | v book.epub | v Kindle Previewer validation / optional KPF conversion | v Upload EPUB or KPF to KDP ``` For most text stories with illustrations, use a **reflowable EPUB**. That means the text adapts to the reader’s device, font size, and screen width, while your pictures appear inline between paragraphs or chapters. Use **fixed-layout EPUB** only if the exact placement of text over images matters, such as a children’s picture book, comic, graphic novel, or heavily designed illustrated book. Fixed layout is more complex and less flexible on Kindle devices. **What The Script Needs** At minimum, the script needs these inputs: ```text story.txt picture1.jpg picture2.jpg ... picture10.jpg metadata.json ``` The `story.txt` should have some way to tell the script where chapters and pictures go. For example: ```text # Chapter 1 Once upon a time... [image: picture1.jpg] The road disappeared into the forest. # Chapter 2 [image: picture2.jpg] The next morning... ``` Or, if your story has no image markers, the script needs a rule like “insert one picture after each chapter” or “insert picture1 after paragraph 5, picture2 after paragraph 10,” etc. A separate metadata file is strongly recommended: ```json { "title": "My Story Title", "author": "Your Name", "language": "en", "publisher": "Your Name", "description": "A short description of the book.", "copyright": "Copyright 2026 Your Name. All rights reserved." } ``` For KDP, you should also prepare a **cover image separately**. Amazon specifically says not to include the cover image inside the manuscript file because KDP adds the cover you provide during title setup. **What The Python Script Should Do** The script should: 1. Read `story.txt` as UTF-8 text. 2. Parse chapter headings, paragraphs, and image markers. 3. Convert plain text into valid XHTML pages. 4. Copy and optimize the images. 5. Generate a table of contents. 6. Generate EPUB package files. 7. Zip everything into a valid `.epub`. 8. Optionally run external validation tools. A valid EPUB is essentially a ZIP file with a required internal structure like this: ```text book.epub ├── mimetype ├── META-INF/ │ └── container.xml └── OEBPS/ ├── content.opf ├── nav.xhtml ├── styles.css ├── chapter1.xhtml ├── chapter2.xhtml └── images/ ├── picture1.jpg ├── picture2.jpg └── ... ``` The important EPUB parts are: `mimetype` Must contain: ```text application/epub+zip ``` This file must be the first file in the ZIP and must not be compressed. `META-INF/container.xml` Tells reading systems where the book package file is. `OEBPS/content.opf` Contains the book metadata, manifest, spine, image list, XHTML file list, and reading order. `OEBPS/nav.xhtml` Contains the EPUB 3 navigation table of contents. `chapter*.xhtml` Contains the actual book content. `styles.css` Controls simple formatting. `images/` Contains your pictures. **Python Libraries I’d Use** For a practical script, use: ```text ebooklib Pillow beautifulsoup4 or lxml python-slugify ``` `ebooklib` handles much of the EPUB packaging. `Pillow` resizes, converts, and validates images. `beautifulsoup4` or `lxml` helps generate or clean XHTML. `python-slugify` helps create safe filenames and IDs. Install example: ```bash pip install ebooklib pillow beautifulsoup4 python-slugify ``` **Image Requirements The Script Should Handle** The script should check that each picture: ```text exists has a normal extension like .jpg, .jpeg, or .png is not corrupt is RGB or safely convertible to RGB has a reasonable pixel size has a reasonable file size has a stable filename with no spaces or unusual characters ``` For Kindle, I would usually convert photos/illustrations to JPEG unless transparency is needed. Use PNG only where transparency or sharp line art matters. The script should probably normalize image names like this: ```text picture1.jpg -> images/picture-001.jpg picture2.png -> images/picture-002.png ``` For reflowable books, images should usually be inserted with CSS like: ```css img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; } ``` Avoid fixed pixel-width text layouts unless you are intentionally making a fixed-layout book. **Important Formatting Rules** The script should avoid: ```text page numbers headers footers manual line breaks at the end of every line text boxes absolute-positioned normal body text a cover image embedded as the first manuscript page ``` Those are common eBook formatting problems. Amazon’s guide specifically notes that eBooks are reflowable, so page numbers, headers, and footers do not apply. The script should create: ```text title page copyright page table of contents chapters optional about-the-author page ``` Example title page XHTML: ```html

My Story Title

by Your Name

``` Example chapter page XHTML: ```html

Chapter 1

Once upon a time...

The road disappeared into the forest.

``` **Validation Tools The Script Should Call** The Python script can create the EPUB, but you should still validate outside Python. Use **Kindle Previewer** to check the result before uploading. Amazon recommends validating EPUB files with Kindle Previewer before upload. Kindle Previewer also has command-line options for conversion, quality checks, logs, and previewing. Conceptually: ```bash kindlepreviewer book.epub -qualitychecks -log -output dist ``` And for conversion: ```bash kindlepreviewer book.epub -convert -output dist ``` The exact executable path depends on where Kindle Previewer is installed. I’d also use EPUBCheck: ```bash java -jar epubcheck.jar book.epub ``` EPUBCheck catches EPUB specification errors; Kindle Previewer catches Kindle-specific rendering and publishing issues. Use both if possible. **A Reasonable Script Interface** I would design the script like this: ```bash python make_kindle_book.py \ --story story.txt \ --images . \ --metadata metadata.json \ --output dist/my-book.epub ``` Optional arguments: ```bash --cover cover.jpg --fixed-layout --image-placement inline --resize-images --validate --kindle-preview ``` But for KDP, I would treat `--cover` carefully: the script can use it for local preview builds, but the KDP upload workflow normally wants the cover supplied separately during title setup. **Minimal Script Skeleton** A real script would be longer, but structurally it needs something like this: ```python from pathlib import Path import json from PIL import Image from ebooklib import epub from bs4 import BeautifulSoup def load_metadata(path): return json.loads(Path(path).read_text(encoding="utf-8")) def optimize_image(src, dst, max_width=1800): dst.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) with Image.open(src) as img: img = img.convert("RGB") if img.width > max_width: ratio = max_width / img.width new_size = (max_width, int(img.height * ratio)) img = img.resize(new_size, Image.LANCZOS) img.save(dst, "JPEG", quality=88, optimize=True) def parse_story(text): chapters = [] current = {"title": "Start", "blocks": []} for line in text.splitlines(): line = line.strip() if not line: continue if line.startswith("# "): if current["blocks"]: chapters.append(current) current = {"title": line[2:].strip(), "blocks": []} elif line.startswith("[image:") and line.endswith("]"): image_name = line[len("[image:"):-1].strip() current["blocks"].append({"type": "image", "src": image_name}) else: current["blocks"].append({"type": "paragraph", "text": line}) if current["blocks"]: chapters.append(current) return chapters def chapter_to_xhtml(chapter, image_map): html = [f"

{chapter['title']}

"] for block in chapter["blocks"]: if block["type"] == "paragraph": html.append(f"

{block['text']}

") elif block["type"] == "image": src = image_map[block["src"]] html.append( f'' ) return "\n".join(html) def build_epub(story_path, metadata_path, output_path): metadata = load_metadata(metadata_path) story_text = Path(story_path).read_text(encoding="utf-8") chapters = parse_story(story_text) book = epub.EpubBook() book.set_identifier(metadata.get("identifier", "my-book")) book.set_title(metadata["title"]) book.set_language(metadata.get("language", "en")) book.add_author(metadata["author"]) css = """ body { font-family: serif; line-height: 1.4; } h1 { text-align: center; page-break-before: always; } figure { margin: 1em 0; text-align: center; } img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; } """ style_item = epub.EpubItem( uid="style", file_name="styles/styles.css", media_type="text/css", content=css, ) book.add_item(style_item) image_map = {} image_items = [] for image_path in sorted(Path(".").glob("picture*.*")): clean_name = f"images/{image_path.stem}.jpg" optimized_path = Path("build") / clean_name optimize_image(image_path, optimized_path) item = epub.EpubItem( uid=image_path.stem, file_name=clean_name, media_type="image/jpeg", content=optimized_path.read_bytes(), ) book.add_item(item) image_items.append(item) image_map[image_path.name] = clean_name epub_chapters = [] for index, chapter in enumerate(chapters, start=1): xhtml = chapter_to_xhtml(chapter, image_map) epub_chapter = epub.EpubHtml( title=chapter["title"], file_name=f"chapter-{index:03}.xhtml", lang=metadata.get("language", "en"), ) epub_chapter.content = xhtml epub_chapter.add_item(style_item) book.add_item(epub_chapter) epub_chapters.append(epub_chapter) book.toc = epub_chapters book.spine = ["nav"] + epub_chapters book.add_item(epub.EpubNcx()) book.add_item(epub.EpubNav()) epub.write_epub(output_path, book) if __name__ == "__main__": build_epub( story_path="story.txt", metadata_path="metadata.json", output_path="book.epub", ) ``` That skeleton is not quite production-ready because it needs stronger XHTML escaping, better image-marker handling, better error messages, and validation integration. But it shows the right structure. **The Main Decision** The biggest thing your script needs is a decision about book type: ```text Mostly text story with pictures between sections: Use reflowable EPUB. Picture book where each page must look exactly designed: Use fixed-layout EPUB or Kindle Create. ``` For your described setup, `story.txt` plus ten pictures, I’d start with a **reflowable EPUB generator** unless the pictures are full-page illustrated spreads where the text placement must be exact. Then validate it in Kindle Previewer, upload the EPUB to KDP, and provide the cover separately in the KDP title setup.
